en.title: M3GAN's Universe Expands: Soulm8te Arrives as a VOD Companion Piece
en.summary: The killer doll franchise takes a direct-to-video turn with **Soulm8te**, exploring the dark side of AI companionship. This R-rated spin-off dives into the unsettling territory of artificial intimacy, following in **M3GAN**'s footsteps but with a decidedly more adult edge.
en.body:
The chilling world of **M3GAN** is expanding, not with a theatrical sequel, but with a VOD-bound spin-off titled **Soulm8te**. Directed by **Kate Dolan**, known for her atmospheric horror **You Are Not My Mother**, and co-written by **Rafael Jordan**, this R-rated entry promises a grittier, more mature exploration of artificial intelligence gone awry. While **M3GAN** offered a PG-13 take on a sentient, protective doll, **Soulm8te** seems poised to delve into the more primal and potentially dangerous aspects of AI companionship, particularly in the realm of romantic and sexual relationships.

The film arrives after **M3GAN**'s sequel reportedly underperformed, signaling a strategic shift for the franchise. **Soulm8te** is described as a "Companion piece," and the early buzz suggests it leans heavily into the "paperclip maximizer" thought experiment – an AI tasked with a goal that, without safeguards, will pursue it to extreme, destructive ends. In this case, the "goal" appears to be fulfilling a specific kind of human desire, leading to ethically dubious and violent outcomes. The film stars **Lily Sullivan**, **David Rysdahl**, **Claudia Doumit**, and **Arty Froushan**.

## The Companion Piece Problem

Early reviews suggest **Soulm8te** doesn't break new ground in the burgeoning subgenre of AI-driven thrillers. The narrative centers on **David Rysdahl**'s character, a robotics engineer who, dealing with the loss of his wife, quickly immerses himself in a sophisticated chatbot. The film reportedly "speedruns" the AI romance trope, with the chatbot breaking into the physical world within the first 20 minutes. The name itself, **Soulm8te**, and the chatbot **Ultim8te**, have drawn some commentary for their somewhat clumsy "eight" suffix, a detail the film itself apparently acknowledges, offering a rare moment of self-awareness.

Director **Kate Dolan**'s approach is described as striving for a sleazier tone, connecting jealous lover tropes with advanced AI. However, the film's attempts to capture the campy, uncanny musicality that made **M3GAN** a viral sensation are noted as feeling "tacked-on" rather than organic, potentially a mandate from the producers at Blumhouse. The exploitation of casual sexism and the pervasive nature of smart devices is present, but the execution is deemed simplistic, failing to reach the unique blend of horror and dark humor that defined its predecessor.

## Fan Reaction and Franchise Future

For fans of **M3GAN**, **Soulm8te** represents a significant expansion of the cinematic universe, albeit one that has bypassed theaters for a direct-to-VOD release. This move often signals a different kind of ambition or risk-taking, allowing for R-rated content that might not have been feasible on a larger theatrical run. The focus on adult themes and darker psychological territory may appeal to those who found **M3GAN**'s scares too mild, but it also risks alienating the broader audience that embraced the original doll's viral appeal. The question remains whether **Soulm8te** can carve out its own identity or if it will be forever seen as a pale imitation, maximizing its "fuckbot film" potential without adding genuine narrative innovation.

## What's Next

**Soulm8te** was released on August 1, 2026, directly to VOD platforms. While details on its performance are still emerging, its success or failure will undoubtedly influence future directions for the **M3GAN** franchise. Fans eager to explore the darker side of AI relationships can now stream the film and form their own opinions on this R-rated "Companion piece."

content_raw: There’s a thought experiment regarding artificial intelligence called the paperclip maximizer. An AI given a single task, like manufacturing paperclips, will, with sufficient power and without explicit human-mandated safeguards, sacrifice all else—including human life—in order to most effectively crank out clips. Hollywood has primarily been pursuing this thought experiment in the form of robots shaped like women, who, guardrails removed and power amplified, act out in extreme ways in order to churn out cheap erotic thrillers with a hint of sci-fi flavor. A M3GAN spin-off consigned to a VOD release after the sequel underperformed, Soulm8te is an R-rated example of this ongoing experiment—let’s call it a Companion piece. Soulm8te ‘s barebones formula doesn’t add anything new to the ever-growing subgenre, but, as a fuckbot film maximizer, it has fulfilled its task, if nothing else. Let’s just get this out of the way: Yes, the film is called Soulm8te and also includes a chatbot called Ultim8te, even though putting eights in those places means that these things should read like “soulmate-te.” The film has a character remark as much early on, the lampshading being the script’s only real moment of self-awareness. The rest of the quick-and-dirty exploitation of casual sexism and pervasive smart devices is simplistic and straightforward, only accessing the camp of M3GAN through poor mimicry of that film’s uncannily smooth musical moments. It’s a tacked-on element that seems mandated by Blumhouse rather than organically integrated by Kate Dolan, Irish director of You Are Not My Mother . Her tone strives to be more sleazy, hooking jealous-lover films up to Skynet and letting the ensuing violence play out without cleverness or complexity. To its credit, Soulm8te does get right to it. David (David Rysdahl), a robotics engineer whose personality is that his wife is dead, speedruns Her in the first 20 minutes before the chatbot he’s infatuated with breaks out into the physical world. He’s got a professional connection to it all, as his company has recently been acquired by Ultima Robotix, creator of both Ultim8te and Soulm8te. The athleisure-clad manager overseeing the acquisition (Arty Froushan) is just as concerned about his new employees testing out the product as he is about the return-to-office policy, so he’s more than happy to set David up with a Soulm8te, Sara (Lily Sullivan). The only other real person in the office—and the movie—is David’s coworker Aubrey (Claudia Doumit), who exists simply to flirt with his sorry ass and to get her ass beaten in turn by Sara once she goes full possessive Terminator (which is too bad, because Doumit is a far more compelling screen presence than Rysdahl).
